section_title: What future does God promise beyond our fragile present life?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands. 2 For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, 3 because when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.

4 For while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life. 5 And it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.

context_lines: Paul continues the contrast between present decline and lasting glory. He pictures present bodily life as an earthly tent that can be dismantled, then speaks of a lasting dwelling from God, not built by human hands.

He adds the image of being clothed. The longing is not simply to shed the body and remain naked, but for mortality to be swallowed up by life. His hope reaches toward the life God gives beyond the weakness and burdens of the present.

God has prepared His people for this purpose and has given the Spirit as a pledge. Paul has used that image already in [2 Corinthians 1:21–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_corinthians/1.htm): the gift received now assures them of what is still to come.

The images give grounds for hope, but they should not be pressed into a detailed account of the materials of a future body or every step between death and resurrection. Paul’s concern is God’s promised life overcoming mortality.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly connect the tent, clothing and lasting dwelling with the promised life God gives beyond death. [Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-corinthians/) and the [USCCB notes on verses 1–5](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/2corinthians/5) both emphasize bodily resurrection rather than a final existence without a body. They discuss details of the clothing image differently, but the longing for mortality to be overcome remains central.
god_plan_lines: [1 Corinthians 15:50–54](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm) explicitly describes the necessary transformation: what is mortal must be clothed with immortality, and death is swallowed up in victory.

That connection places Paul’s longing within the resurrection Christ promises His people. God’s purpose goes beyond helping them tolerate a failing body; it includes life in which mortality no longer has the final word. The Spirit’s present gift supports waiting for that completion.
